precepts.text: The land beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles; the east-side territory became known as the land of the Gentiles.
precepts.point: That region became known as the land of the Gentiles, as you read in the gospel.

note.label: Joshua 12: The Thirty and One Kings

precepts.why:
Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan were smitten by Moses and the children of Israel, and Moses gave their land “for a possession unto the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh.” Look up a map of the Jordan river and the twelve tribes and you will see the split of where Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh dwelt, on the east side of Jordan.

That region became known as the land of the Gentiles, as you read in the gospel: “The land of Zabulon, and the land of Nephthalim, by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles”. Beyond Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the east-side territory on the other side Jordan toward the rising of the sun.

precepts.text: We descend from the famous men of the book of the Lord.
precepts.point: Take pride in this: we are the descendants of the most famous men on the face of the earth. Our forefathers are mentioned in every single nation, and everybody wants to lay claim to them and to our book. That is why all nations hate us, and we will be famous again: the Most High will get Israel praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame, when he turns back our captivity before our eyes. Remember, Jerusalem is a people before it is a place.

note.label: Joshua 12: The Thirty and One Kings

precepts.why:
In Ecclesiasticus Joshua is called “Jesus the son a Nave”, for Joshua translated into the Greek is Jesus, and Nave is Nun: Joshua the son of Nun. He “was valiant in the wars, and was the successor of Moses in prophecies, who according to his name was made great for the saving of the elect of God, and taking vengeance of the enemies that rose up against them, that he might set Israel in their inheritance.”

“How great glory gat he, when he did lift up his hands, and stretched out his sword against the cities! Who before him so stood to it? for the Lord himself brought his enemies unto him. Did not the sun go back by his means? and was not one day as long as two?” He said, Sun, be thou still, and there were two days of sunlight on the earth. “He called upon the most high Lord, when the enemies pressed upon him on every side; and the great Lord heard him.”

“And with hailstones of mighty power he made the battle to fall violently upon the nations, and in the descent of Beth-horon he destroyed them that resisted, that the nations might know all their strength, because he fought in the sight of the Lord, and he followed the Mighty One.” That is the fame of the man who smote thirty and one kings.

note.label: Joshua 12: The Thirty and One Kings

precepts.why:
His counterpart Caleb was a mighty man too. “In the time of Moses also he did a work of mercy, he and Caleb the son of Jephunne, in that they withstood the congregation, and withheld the people from sin, and appeased the wicked murmuring. And of six hundred thousand people on foot, they two were preserved to bring them in to the heritage, even unto the land that floweth with milk and honey.”

“The Lord gave strength also unto Caleb, which remained with him unto his old age: so that he entered upon the high places of the land, and his seed obtained it for an heritage: That all the children of Israel might see that it is good to follow the Lord.” The Most High gave Caleb strength unto his old age, fighting in his eighties like he was in his twenties, and you will read of his strength in the next few chapters. Joshua and Caleb, the two preserved of six hundred thousand, that all Israel might see it is good to follow the Lord.

precepts.text: I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame, when I turn back your captivity before your eyes; Israel will be famous again.

note.label: Joshua 12: The Thirty and One Kings

precepts.why:
We will be famous again. “In that day it shall be said to Jerusalem, Fear thou not: and to Zion, Let not thine hands be slack. The Lord thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.” Remember, Jerusalem is a people before it is a place.

“Behold, at that time I will undo all that afflict thee: and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will get them praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame. At that time will I bring you again, even in the time that I gather you: for I will make you a name and a praise among all people of the earth, when I turn back your captivity before your eyes, saith the Lord.”

The Most High will get Israel praise and fame in every land where they have been put to shame, when he turns back our captivity before our eyes. We are the descendants of the most famous men on the face of the earth, the men who took thirty and one kings, and we will be a name and a praise among all people of the earth again.

note.label: Judges 1: Judah Goes Up First, but the Inhabitants Are Not Driven Out

precepts.why: “Now these are the kings of the land, which the children of Israel smote, and possessed their land”. What follows is the record of the kings Israel struck down in the wars we just finished reading in Joshua. The king of Jerusalem is counted among them, so Jerusalem’s king had already fallen in Joshua’s day; the fight here in Judges is Judah taking the city itself, smiting it with the edge of the sword and setting it on fire.

precepts.text: The king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; Jerusalem's king was already counted among the kings smitten.
precepts.point: The king of Jerusalem was already among the kings of the land which the children of Israel smote and whose land they possessed, so this fight in Judges is Judah taking the city itself.

note.label: Judges 1: Judah Goes Up First, but the Inhabitants Are Not Driven Out

precepts.why: “The king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one”. Jerusalem’s king was already counted among the kings of the land which the children of Israel smote and whose land they possessed. So this is not the first time Israel faced Jerusalem: the king had fallen in Joshua’s wars, and now the children of Judah went against the city itself, took it, smote it with the edge of the sword and set it on fire. Even so, the Jebusites who dwelt in it were not driven out.
